strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in long-context LLM inference: quadratic prefill attention cost. The proposed Token Sparse Attention is conceptually simple and appealing, selecting tokens per head, running dense attention on the compressed token set, and scattering outputs back so tokens can be reconsidered in later layers.

The method is designed to compose with existing optimized dense and sparse attention implementations. This compatibility is practically valuable, and the experiments show additive attention-speed gains when combined with FlashAttention, Minference, and FlexPrefill.

The paper provides useful diagnostic motivation for layer-wise and head-wise token-importance variation, and introduces a reasonable sparse-layer selection heuristic based on inter-layer representation drift.

The empirical evaluation covers two long-context models, multiple context lengths up to 128K/256K, and several benchmarks including RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack. The main results generally preserve accuracy while improving measured attention latency.
The comparison against token-eviction methods is relevant: under similar reported speedups, the reversible token-sparse approach preserves RULER accuracy better than FastKV and GemFilter.
weaknesses: The measured gains are mostly attention-latency gains rather than end-to-end inference gains. Since prefill includes non-attention computation, token scoring, indexing, gather/scatter, memory movement, and decoding costs, the practical wall-clock benefit is not fully established. The headline speedups therefore overstate the demonstrated system impact.

The empirical scope is narrower than the claims suggest. Only two models are evaluated, both decoder-only long-context instruction models, and all implementation results are on a single A100 80GB setup. There is no evidence for portability across hardware, larger models, different architectures, or production inference settings.

The contribution is incremental relative to existing sparse attention and token selection work. The main novelty is the compress-attend-scatter design with dynamic coverage and drift-based layer selection, but many components resemble prior heavy-hitter/token-pruning/sparse-attention ideas. The paper should more sharply separate what is technically new from recombination of known mechanisms.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The method is described as allowing skipped tokens to be reconsidered, but unselected tokens do not receive attention updates in the sparse layer; they are only preserved through the residual path. This is less reversible than the framing implies and may matter for tasks requiring layer-local contextual updates.

The selection and layer-sparsification heuristics are under-validated. The inter-layer drift criterion is supported mainly by a correlation experiment on RULER with random 3-layer sparsification, but there is little analysis of whether the selected layers generalize across tasks, prompts, models, or hyperparameter settings. The fixed delta=0.5 choice is not justified strongly.

The baselines and comparisons leave open fairness questions. FlexPrefill, Minference, FastKV, and GemFilter have their own tunable hyperparameters, but the paper gives limited detail on tuning budgets, whether baselines were optimized for the same latency-accuracy objective, and whether the proposed method was tuned on evaluation benchmarks.

Several reported improvements are modest. For example, adding Token Sparse to FlexPrefill improves LLaMA 128K attention speedup from 2.44x to 2.76x with nearly unchanged accuracy, and on InfiniteBench it often slightly decreases average accuracy. This is useful but not yet a compelling advance without stronger end-to-end measurements.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript mentions a Triton scoring kernel and integration with FlashAttention but does not provide enough low-level details about kernels, exact latency measurement protocol, warmup, batching, sequence construction, hyperparameter search, or code release plans for others to reliably reproduce the results.

Presentation has some issues. The appendix Needle-in-a-Haystack figure appears to have an incorrect caption referring to an attention latency breakdown, and some table/figure discussion is terse. The limitations section is present but relatively shallow and does not discuss possible failure modes beyond aggressive sparsification or the risk of benchmark-specific tuning.

Research ethics are not materially discussed. While this is a systems/inference paper with limited direct ethical risk, the paper should still briefly address energy/resource implications, deployment tradeoffs, and risks from accuracy degradation in long-context applications.

strengths: The paper identifies a real bottleneck in long-context prefill and proposes a simple, implementation-friendly idea: per-head token selection followed by dense attention over the selected subset, then scattering outputs back to the full sequence so later layers can reconsider skipped tokens.

The motivation that token importance varies by layer and head is plausible and supported by diagnostic plots; the method is positioned clearly as complementary to block-sparse attention rather than as a replacement.

The empirical section covers multiple long-context benchmarks and two public models, and it includes useful comparisons against FlashAttention, Minference, FlexPrefill, fixed sparsity, and token-eviction methods.
The limitation section acknowledges smaller gains at short contexts and possible accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsification.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not convincingly substantiated because speedups are reported mainly as attention-latency speedups at 128K, not end-to-end prefill or full inference latency. The standalone gains over FlashAttention are modest, e.g. 1.36x for LLaMA and 1.22x for Mistral on RULER, and the incremental gain on top of FlexPrefill is also modest, e.g. 2.44x to 2.76x for LLaMA. This weakens the practical significance of claims such as substantial scalable inference improvement.

Accuracy results are often neutral or negative rather than clearly improved. On InfiniteBench and LongBench, adding Token Sparse Attention frequently reduces average performance, especially with FlexPrefill and Minference. The paper still frames the method as consistently improving the accuracy-latency trade-off, but the evidence mostly shows small speed gains bought with small accuracy drops.

The method description leaves important reproducibility gaps. The number of recent queries used for scoring, exact sparse-layer selection procedure and calibration data, benchmark sample settings, latency measurement protocol, baseline hyperparameters for FastKV/GemFilter, random seeds, and Triton kernel details are not specified sufficiently for reliable reproduction.

The dynamic layer selection may depend on calibration tasks or data, but the paper does not clearly state how drift is estimated without test leakage or how robust the chosen layers are across domains. The fixed choice delta=0.5 is not justified beyond one correlation plot.

The technical novelty appears incremental. The core operation is token pruning inside selected attention layers with residual preservation, combined with a token-importance heuristic. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from nearby token-pruning, prompt-compression, and sparse-attention approaches beyond the reversible scatter-back framing.

The comparison to token-eviction methods is narrow: only LLaMA on RULER, only one matched-speed setting, and limited details about baseline tuning. This is not enough to support broad claims that reversible interleaving is superior to eviction-based methods.

The paper lacks important ablations isolating the contribution of per-head selection, dynamic token coverage, sparse-layer selection, recent-query scoring, and scatter-back/residual preservation. Without these, it is hard to know which design choice actually drives the reported results.

Presentation has several rough edges that reduce confidence: terminology around token coverage is confusing because very small tau values produce large sparsity; some figure/table captions appear mismatched or under-informative, e.g. the Needle-in-a-Haystack appendix caption repeats a latency-breakdown caption; and many plots are described qualitatively without numerical details in the text.

The limitations and ethics discussion is incomplete. The paper does not discuss risks from approximate attention in high-stakes long-context settings, potential benchmark-specific failures, or the environmental/computational cost of extra scoring and calibration, even though the proposed method deliberately drops context-dependent computation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in long-context LLM inference: prefill attention cost. The proposed token-level compress-attend-decompress mechanism is simple, practically motivated, and plausibly complementary to existing dense and sparse attention kernels.

The core idea is technically appealing because it avoids irreversible token eviction: skipped tokens remain in the residual stream and can be reconsidered in later layers. The manuscript supports this motivation with evidence that token importance varies substantially across layers and heads.

The evaluation is fairly broad for a systems/efficiency paper, covering two long-context models, RULER, InfiniteBench, and appendix results on LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack. Results generally show improved attention speedups with small accuracy changes, especially when combined with FlexPrefill and FlashAttention.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline numbers, including dynamic versus fixed sparsity, comparison to token-eviction methods under roughly matched speedup, sparsity as a function of context length, and latency-overhead breakdowns.

The method is likely useful in practice because it appears modular: the selected QKV tensors remain dense, allowing reuse of optimized attention kernels rather than requiring a wholly new sparse kernel stack.
weaknesses: The efficiency evidence is somewhat under-specified and may overstate practical impact. The main speedups are attention speedups at 128K rather than full end-to-end prefill or generation latency, and the paper does not consistently report wall-clock latency, memory traffic, batching behavior, or throughput under realistic serving settings.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The manuscript gives high-level hyperparameters and hardware, but key implementation details of the Triton scoring kernel, indexing/compression overhead, exact layer selections, benchmark settings, and baseline configurations are not sufficient to independently reproduce the reported trade-offs without code.

Several important ablations are missing or thin: the contribution of compress-decompress versus dynamic token coverage versus drift-based layer selection is not fully isolated; head-wise selection is motivated but not directly ablated against shared per-layer token sets; and sensitivity to the number of recent queries used for scoring is not reported.

The comparison to prior methods is useful but not fully convincing as a decisive benchmark. FastKV and GemFilter are evaluated only on RULER with one model, while the strongest complementary gains over FlexPrefill are sometimes modest and can include small accuracy losses on InfiniteBench and Mistral.

Some claims are broader than the evidence. For example, “fully compatible” with dense and sparse attention kernels is demonstrated for a small set of methods, and extension to decoding or multimodal settings is speculative. The paper should more clearly delimit what has actually been implemented and measured.

Presentation has a few issues that reduce confidence: appendix text around Needle-in-a-Haystack appears mismatched with a latency-breakdown caption, some figures/tables lack enough numerical detail in the extracted manuscript, and there are minor writing/formatting problems. These are fixable but noticeable.

Limitations are acknowledged, but the discussion is narrow. There is little treatment of failure modes where sparse token selection might systematically drop rare but important evidence, nor any research ethics discussion beyond efficiency benefits and accuracy trade-offs.

strengths: The paper identifies a real limitation of prior token-eviction approaches: token importance varies substantially across layers and heads, so irreversible early pruning is a poor fit for long-context prefill. The proposed compress-attend-decompress design is a clear and useful alternative that preserves the possibility of reselecting tokens in later layers.

The method is practically motivated and largely compatible with existing optimized attention implementations. The paper demonstrates composition with FlashAttention, MInference, FlexPrefill, SeerAttention, and X-Attention, which supports the claim that the method is complementary rather than a replacement for sparse attention kernels.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this topic: two long-context models, RULER and InfiniteBench in the main paper, additional LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack results, comparisons to eviction and non-eviction baselines, dynamic-vs-fixed sparsity ablations, scoring ablations, drift-based layer-selection ablations, and A100/A6000 latency measurements.

The reported accuracy-efficiency trade-off is credible and useful in the 128K regime. For example, on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Token Sparse improves FlashAttention prefill speed at 128K from 31.04s to 24.35s with nearly unchanged RULER average accuracy, and improves FlexPrefill latency from 18.45s to 16.81s.

The presentation is generally clear: the method is decomposed into token coverage, per-head token selection, compression/decompression, and sparse layer selection, with helpful figures and targeted ablations.
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claims are somewhat overstated relative to the practical end-to-end gains. The abstract emphasizes up to 3.23x attention speedup, but the main prefill latency gains are much smaller: around 1.24-1.27x over FlashAttention at 128K, and the method is slower at 8K. The distinction between attention-level speedup, prefill speedup, and user-visible inference speed should be clearer and more central.

The method leaves decoding dense and keeps the full KV cache, so it does not address the memory/bandwidth bottleneck of long-context decoding. This substantially limits the overall significance for full LLM serving, especially when many generated tokens are requested.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper mentions a custom Triton kernel but gives no code release, kernel details, batching constraints, exact recent-query window size, seeds, benchmark sampling details, or enough implementation information to reproduce the reported latencies. Hardware is reported, but software versions and baseline implementation details are sparse.

The algorithmic description has ambiguities. The token coverage parameter tau is described as pruning least-important tokens whose cumulative mass exceeds tau, yet very small tau values such as 0.005 lead to very large reported sparsities at long contexts; this may be plausible under a long-tail distribution, but the paper should make the semantics and resulting retained-token counts explicit. The pooling operation and last_q are also underspecified.

The central mechanism means unselected tokens skip the attention sublayer in sparse layers and only pass through via the residual path. The paper says this preserves information and allows later reconsideration, but it does not fully analyze the representational effect of repeatedly skipping attention updates for many tokens, nor when this can fail beyond aggregate benchmark numbers.

The evaluation is mostly on two instruction-tuned models and standard long-context benchmarks, several of which are synthetic or retrieval-heavy. The method's robustness on more model families, larger models, real serving batches, diverse prompt distributions, and generation-heavy workloads remains uncertain.

The limitations and impact statements are brief. The limitations mention short-context inefficiency and aggressive sparsification, but do not discuss reproducibility, full-KV memory cost, decoding limitations, benchmark narrowness, or possible failure modes when pruned tokens contain rare but essential information.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in long-context inference: prefill attention cost at 64K-128K+ contexts. The proposed compress-attend-decompress mechanism is conceptually simple and has a plausible advantage over permanent token eviction because skipped tokens can be reconsidered in later layers.

The evaluation covers multiple long-context benchmarks and two 128K-context models, and the authors test composition with several sparse attention baselines rather than only comparing against dense FlashAttention. The appendix adds useful ablations for scoring method, drift-based layer selection, delta selection, and prefill latency on A100/A6000.

The reported results suggest a potentially useful engineering trade-off in the intended long-context regime: modest end-to-end prefill speedups at 128K with relatively small average accuracy changes on RULER, InfiniteBench, and LongBench. The comparison to token-eviction methods is also directionally supportive of the reversible design.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not fully supported by the presented evidence. Many headline gains are attention-level speedups rather than end-to-end speedups; the end-to-end TTFT gains are much smaller, and the method can slow down inference at 8K. The abstract's emphasis on up to 3.23x attention speedup risks overstating practical impact.

Key methodological details are underspecified, which hurts reproducibility and soundness: the number of recent queries, exact pooling operation, Triton scoring kernel behavior, handling of variable per-head token sets, gather/scatter overheads, layer-selection preprocessing data, and full baseline configurations are not described sufficiently for reliable replication.

The layer-selection procedure may involve tuning on task/context distributions close to the evaluation setting. The paper says drift is measured across tasks and context lengths and then used as a preprocessing step, but it does not clearly separate calibration data from evaluation data, raising a possible benchmark leakage or overfitting concern.

The accuracy claims are sometimes stronger than the tables justify. InfiniteBench and LongBench show consistent small degradations for several compositions, and RULER differences are often within a very small margin without confidence intervals or repeated-task variance. The paper repeatedly says performance is preserved, but uncertainty is not quantified.

The novelty is incremental. Token selection, prompt/token pruning, attention sparsification, and non-eviction token selection are already active areas; this work's main distinction is per-head QKV-level reversible selection plus composition with sparse kernels. That is interesting, but not clearly a major conceptual advance without stronger systems evidence.

The practical implementation story is incomplete. The paper claims compatibility with FlashAttention and sparse kernels, yet the method requires token scoring, per-head top-k selection, QKV gathering, output scattering, and custom Triton support. There is no code availability statement, kernel pseudocode, memory-footprint analysis, or discussion of batching/serving behavior.

Limitations and ethics are minimal. The limitations section notes short-context weakness and aggressive sparsification risk, but does not discuss calibration leakage, reproducibility barriers, deployment constraints, energy/cost trade-offs, or failure modes where pruned attention could systematically harm tasks requiring diffuse evidence across the context.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck: long-context prefill attention. The proposed compress-attend-decompress design is technically sensible because it preserves the full residual stream while allowing per-layer and per-head token reselection, directly addressing a real weakness of irreversible token eviction methods.

The method is appealingly compatible with existing attention implementations. The experiments show it can be composed with FlashAttention, MInference, FlexPrefill, SeerAttention, and X-Attention, which strengthens the claim that the contribution is complementary rather than a replacement for a particular sparse kernel.

The evaluation is fairly broad for this area: two long-context instruction models, RULER and InfiniteBench in the main text, plus LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, additional sparse-attention baselines, and OrthoRank in the appendix. The paper also reports both attention-level speedups and full prefill latency on A100 and A6000 GPUs.

The empirical results are convincing overall: accuracy is usually preserved within a small margin while attention or prefill speed improves at long contexts. The comparison against token-eviction methods under matched speedups is particularly useful and supports the central motivation for reversible/interleaved selection.

The ablations are meaningful. The paper studies recent-query scoring, fixed versus dynamic sparsity, drift-based layer selection, and delta sweeps, giving reasonable evidence that the main design choices matter rather than being arbitrary.

Presentation is generally clear, with intuitive figures for layer/head token-importance dynamics and a readable method description. The limitations section acknowledges reduced benefit at short context lengths and degradation under overly aggressive sparsification.
weaknesses: The novelty is useful but somewhat incremental: the method combines token selection, attention-score-based importance, and selective layer sparsification in a clean way, but it does not introduce a fundamentally new attention algorithm or theoretical insight. Its main value is practical composition and engineering effectiveness.

The strongest speedup claims are mostly in attention-level measurements, while end-to-end prefill gains are more modest. For example, Token Sparse over FlashAttention gives about 1.27x prefill speedup at 128K on A100, not the larger attention-only numbers emphasized in the abstract and figures. The paper could better foreground the practical latency gains.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. The method depends on a custom Triton scoring kernel and integration details for several sparse-attention systems, but there is no clear code release, pseudocode is high level, and several implementation choices are underspecified, such as recent-query window size, pooling variants, exact selected layers per model, batching assumptions, and kernel overhead details.

The evaluation uses only two models, both in the 8B-12B range. It is unclear whether the approach scales similarly to larger models, different architectures, multimodal models, or production serving conditions with batching, varied prompt distributions, and memory pressure.

Some experimental choices appear tuned or calibrated on the evaluated setting. The drift-based layer selection threshold, token coverage values, and FlexPrefill/MInference configurations may interact with model and benchmark characteristics; the paper would be stronger with a clearer validation protocol separating hyperparameter selection from final evaluation.

The ethics/impact statement is generic and does not meaningfully discuss possible societal or deployment implications of cheaper long-context inference, such as increased capacity for large-scale processing of sensitive documents. This is not a central flaw, but it is underdeveloped.
